displayQuote: A society gets all the criminals it deserves

meta.title: Who really said "A society gets all the criminals it deserves"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Emma Goldman’s line — she was quoting it. It belongs to the French criminologist Alexandre Lacassagne, via Havelock Ellis’s The Criminal (1890).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A society gets all the criminals it deserves'?
meta.ogDescription: Goldman quoted it; she did not write it. The line is Alexandre Lacassagne’s, reported by Havelock Ellis in The Criminal (1890).

answer.label: Not Emma Goldman — actually Alexandre Lacassagne
answer.sourceLine: Goldman does quote the line — in Prisons: A Social Crime and Failure, in Anarchism and Other Essays — but she quotes it as somebody else’s, and says so on the page. Her own text names Lacassagne, and her footnote names her intermediary: Havelock Ellis’s The Criminal (1890) ↗, where the sentence appears in Lacassagne’s mouth.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Prisons: A Social Crime and Failure
Anarchism and Other Essays, 2nd revised ed. (1911), p. 122
Alexandre Lacassagne (1843–1924), founder of the Lyon school of criminology

source.excerpt: There is close relation, says Havelock Ellis, between crimes against the person and the price of alcohol, between crimes against property and the price of wheat. He quotes Quetelet and Lacassagne, the former looking upon society as the preparer of crime, and the criminals as instruments that execute them. The latter finds that “the social environment is the cultivation medium of criminality; that the criminal is the microbe, an element which only becomes important when it finds the medium which causes it to ferment; every society has the criminals it deserves.”
trail: We read Goldman’s essay in the primary text: English Wikisource’s transcription of Anarchism and Other Essays, 2nd revised edition (1911) ↗. The passage stands on page 122 ↗, with the footnote to Ellis.

We then read Goldman’s source. Havelock Ellis, The Criminal (1890) ↗ has it as: “The social environment,” Lacassagne has well said, “is the cultivation medium of criminality; the criminal is the microbe … every society has the criminals that it deserves.”

The same book returns to the thought later in its own voice — “so true it is that every society has only the criminals that it deserves” — which is where the “only” that sometimes appears in circulation comes from.
source.cutTag: Goldman, Anarchism and Other Essays (1911), p. 122
source.excerptNote: “The latter” is Lacassagne. Goldman sets the closing clause in italics and attaches a footnote reading simply “The Criminal” — Ellis’s book. The popular version, “a society gets all the criminals it deserves”, matches neither Goldman’s wording nor Ellis’s.

author.name: Alexandre Lacassagne
author.heading: About Alexandre Lacassagne
author.bio: Alexandre Lacassagne founded the Lyon school of criminology, the main rival to Lombroso’s Italian school and influential from about 1885 to 1914. Against the idea that criminals are born recognisable, he argued that crime is made by circumstances — a position he compressed into the image of the criminal as a microbe and society as the medium that lets him multiply. He was also a pioneer of forensic medicine.

copyAttribution: "Every society has the criminals it deserves." — Alexandre Lacassagne, quoted by Havelock Ellis in The Criminal (1890), and quoted from Ellis by Emma Goldman in "Prisons: A Social Crime and Failure," Anarchism and Other Essays, 2nd rev. ed. (1911), p. 122. Not Goldman’s own line: she cites it as Lacassagne’s on the page. The popular wording "a society gets all the criminals it deserves" appears in neither primary text.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The line is credited to Goldman for the ordinary reason: it appears in a famous essay of hers, and quotation collectors took the surrounding name. Reading one more sentence of that essay settles it.

items.why: It sits inside her essay Prisons: A Social Crime and Failure, but inside quotation marks, introduced by “the latter finds that” and footnoted to Ellis. The page says so ↗.
Ellis is where Goldman found it, and he is sometimes credited in her place. But his own text ↗ introduces it with “Lacassagne has well said”.
Both primary texts read “every society has the criminals it deserves”. “A society gets all the criminals it deserves” is a later, looser rewording that appears in neither.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence belongs to Alexandre Lacassagne ↗, reported by Ellis in 1890 and quoted by Goldman in 1911 — each of them scrupulously crediting the one before.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Lacassagne ran the Lyon school of criminology, and his quarrel was with Cesare Lombroso, who held that criminals were a biological type you could identify by the shape of a skull. Lacassagne’s answer was the microbe image: the criminal is nothing without the medium he ferments in, and the medium is society.

That is why Goldman wanted it. Her essay argues that prisons fail because they treat crime as a defect in the prisoner rather than as a product of the arrangement that made him — and a French criminologist had already put it in one sentence.
detailsBody: The chain is unusually well documented because all three writers were careful. Ellis names Lacassagne, Goldman names Lacassagne and footnotes Ellis, and only the quotation books dropped the attribution — which is the ordinary way a line changes hands.
context.pull: The criminal is the microbe; society is the medium he ferments in.

sourcesVerified.claim: Goldman’s essay quotes the line as Lacassagne’s, introduced by “The latter finds that” and footnoted to The Criminal; the printed page is 122 of the 1911 2nd revised edition.
The full essay text carries the same passage and footnote.

Ellis’s The Criminal (1890) reads: “The social environment,” Lacassagne has well said, “… every society has the criminals that it deserves.” It also later says “every society has only the criminals that it deserves”.
Alexandre Lacassagne (1843–1924) was a French physician and criminologist who founded the Lyon school of criminology, the main rival to Lombroso’s Italian school.
